title: Israel's UBQ turns household garbage into a plastic material, from which Mercedes parts and McDonald's trays are made

trailer.text: Jack (Tato) Bigio immigrated to Israel from Peru in 1984, and in 2012 he founded UBQ with partners.
According to Globes, the company found a way to turn household waste into organic plastic.
According to the Jerusalem Post, the company is based in Kibbutz Tze'elim, and there it developed a way to turn unsorted household waste into thermoplastic.
According to Calcalist, Daimler makes from this material a battery housing for Mercedes' new electric cars.
In 2024 the company opened a full-scale production facility in Bergen op Zoom, the Netherlands.

glance.label: Founders
glance.value: Jack Bigio, Yehuda Pearl, Eran Lev

glance.label: Where
glance.value: Kibbutz Tze'elim, and Bergen op Zoom in the Netherlands

paragraphs.text: According to Globes, in Israel more than 90% of the garbage goes to landfill and not to recycling.
According to the World Economic Forum, almost 70% of household waste is sent to landfill or dumped in the open.
According to Calcalist, 60% of household waste is organic material, mainly food scraps.
According to Bigio, mixed garbage goes to landfill or to incineration, and this has severe side effects.
According to him, the garbage eventually breaks down into toxic methane gas.
According to Calcalist, landfills cause water and air pollution because of the methane gas they emit.

According to the Algemeiner, the UBQ founders' initiative "was also proposed" by the Environmental Ministry, which called for cutting the amount of waste buried underground by 20%, but the article does not clarify what this means.
Bigio was born in Peru, and at 18 he came to Israel in 1984 to study at the Hebrew University.
He said that in 2010, during a "break" year in which he advised start-ups, he met a company that inspired him.
According to him, he was told the task was impossible: to turn garbage into a single homogeneous material that meets strict quality standards and is attractively priced for the consumer.
Bigio met with Prof. Oded Shoseyov of the Hebrew University, and Shoseyov told him the idea was possible at the chemical level.
UBQ was founded in 2012 by Yehuda Pearl, Jack Bigio and Eran Lev.
According to Algemeiner, Eran Lev is a lawyer and an El Al pilot.
Albert Douer, a Jewish-Colombian financier, is a key figure in the company.
UBQ's leading investors include Sabra founder Yehuda Pearl, Albert Douer and Scott Tobin, a partner at Battery Ventures.
According to Calcalist, Yehuda Pearl is a Jewish-American investor, and he is the main investor in UBQ.
Jerusalem Post: in 2019

stations.title: Years of quiet work, and how it works

paragraphs.text: According to Jewish News, the company carried out nearly seven years of testing in stealth mode.
According to the Jerusalem Post, it emerged from stealth mode to unveil its solution.
According to Calcalist, the mixture is transferred to a reactor that applies physical pressures and builds a matrix.
According to Bigio, UBQ works at a heat of 200 degrees Celsius, while plastic from oil is made at a heat of 800 to 1200 degrees.
According to UBQ, every ton of finished material requires 1.45 tons of raw waste.
According to Douer, a color limitation prevents UBQ products from being white or transparent.
According to Bigio, new products will contain between 15% and 60% of UBQ's material.
According to Jewish News, the material is not approved for direct food contact, but it has many uses in the food industry.

stations.title: What is made from the garbage

paragraphs.text: According to Jewish News, the Israeli company partnered with Mercedes-Benz in making vehicle parts.
According to Calcalist, Germany's Daimler makes from the material the battery housing in Mercedes' new electric cars.
According to the Jerusalem Post, UBQ contracted with Arcos Dorados, the world's largest McDonald's franchisee, which has 2,200 restaurants.
According to Bigio, McDonald's began replacing the trays at 30 central branches in Brazil, and the move will later be expanded.
According to Bigio, UBQ supplies the Italian company Mainetti with containers of the material, from which it makes ecological hangers.

According to the Jerusalem Post, as of the article's publication, the Central Virginia Waste Management Authority was to distribute to residents "next month", in the company's first collaboration with authorities in the US, an initial order of 2,000 recycling bins made from UBQ's material.
According to Algemeiner, in Israel UBQ works with the Keter Group and with Carmel Olefins of the Bazan Group.
According to UBQ's sustainability manager, the material is cheaper than oil-based plastic.
According to Algemeiner, the company sells it to various industries at a price similar to traditional plastic.
According to Globes, UBQ has raised $250 million to date, and it has well-known clients in Israel and worldwide.
According to Calcalist, UBQ bought land near Amsterdam to build a plant that would collect garbage from Europe.
According to Jewish Independent, the company opened a second, much bigger plant in the Netherlands.
According to ERM, UBQ inaugurated an industrial factory in Bergen op Zoom in early 2024.

According to the Jerusalem Post, ahead of the launch of the plant in the Netherlands, UBQ announced its intention to triple its workforce by hiring 140 full-time employees, 80 of them in operating roles at the new laboratory and production facility in the Netherlands.
According to ChemAnalyst, the company expects to create about 140 new jobs by 2025, including for people with disabilities.
UBQ announced on September 30, 2024 that it had received a €5 million grant from the European Union's Just Transition Fund.

stations.title: What the numbers say, and who recognized it

paragraphs.text: The Swiss firm Quantis conducted a life cycle assessment for UBQ, and it points to a benefit for the climate.
According to the Jerusalem Post, the sustainability consultancy Quantis International called the material “the most climate-positive material on the planet”.

According to the ERM summary, the cradle-to-gate carbon footprint (from raw materials to the factory gate) of UBQ pellets produced in Bergen op Zoom is minus 1.02 kg CO2eq per kg. The figure is based on projected design data, and the negative value results from temporary storage of biogenic carbon (minus 1.17 kg), which is released at the end of the product's life.
An independent expert, Dr. Matt Fishwick, verified ERM's life cycle assessment.
According to Algemeiner, each ton of UBQ plastic reduces 12 tons of carbon dioxide over 20 years.
According to the Jerusalem Post, an industrial UBQ facility with a capacity of 80,000 tons per year is equivalent to taking more than 565,000 cars off the road each year.
In 2023 UBQ was included in Time magazine's list of the best inventions.
According to Globes, most of the workers at the Tze'elim plant live along the Gaza Strip.
According to Bigio, Bedouins, Russians and Israelis work together at UBQ.

According to Calcalist, at the time the article was published, when the Tze'elim plant was defined as a pilot plant, the company employed 35 people between the plant in Tze'elim and the offices in Tel Aviv.
According to Calcalist, at the time the article was published, only two waste trucks a week arrived at the small recycling plant in Tze'elim, supplying it with 5,000 tons a year.
According to Globes, the two senior workers were murdered on October 7 at Kfar Azza.
Bigio said the company went back to work three weeks after October 7.
Bigio said he wants UBQ to be a global Israeli company, like Teva or Netafim.
According to Globes: an assistant controller and a chief engineer, murdered at Kfar Azza
Prof. Ofira Ayalon of the Technion visited the plant, and according to her she came away with many doubts about the technology.
According to Calcalist, UBQ denies using binding agents.
According to Calcalist, UBQ's plastic cannot yet be used for packaging and containers for storing food.
According to Calcalist, about 15 years before the article was published, Yuval Tamir began developing a technology for turning Kishon sludge into a plastic material.
UBQ confirms that it bought patents from him, but emphasizes that its material and technology are different.
According to Calcalist, the company claims that a team of advising scientists developed the technology over seven years.
According to Calcalist, Yehuda Pearl bought the intellectual property of Nova Arena.
